Hirohito: Emperor Shōwa (born Hirohito; 29 April 1901 – 7 January 1989) was Emperor of Japan from 25 December 1926 until his death in 1989.

Mohammed bin Salman: Mohammed is the first child of King Salman bin Abdulaziz and his third wife, Fahda bint Falah Al Hithlain.
In what year did Fidel Castro die?
Fidel Castro: Born in Birán, the son of a wealthy Spanish farmer, Castro adopted leftist and anti-imperialist ideas while studying law at the University of Havana.

Mikhail Gorbachev: Born in Privolnoye, North Caucasus Krai, into a peasant family of Russian and Ukrainian heritage, Gorbachev grew up under the rule of Joseph Stalin.

Louis XV (15 February 1710 – 10 May 1774), known as Louis the Beloved (French: le Bien-Aimé), was King of France from 1 September 1715 until his death in 1774.
In what year was Italian Social Republic founded?
Italian Social Republic: The German occupation triggered widespread national resistance against it and the Italian Social Republic during the liberation of Italy and the Italian civil war.

Republican Party (United States): The Republican Party, also known as the Grand Old Party (GOP), is a right-wing to far-right political party in the United States.

In which country did the Battle of the Camel take place?
Battle of the Camel: Iraq. The Battle of the Camel, also known as the Battle of Basra (Arabic: معركة الجمل, romanized: Maʿrakat al-Jamal) took place in 656 CE outside of Basra in Iraq.
In which country is Republican Proposal based?
Republican Proposal: Argentina. Republican Proposal (Spanish: Propuesta Republicana), usually referred to by its abbreviation PRO, is a political party in Argentina.
In which country was the Caliphate of Córdoba?
Caliphate of Córdoba: Spain. The Emirate of Córdoba, and from 929, the Caliphate of Córdoba, was an Arab Islamic state ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 756 to 1031.
In which country was the Sultanate of Ternate?
Sultanate of Ternate: Indonesia. The Ternate kingdom was established by Momole Cico, the first leader of Ternate, with the title Baab Mashur Malamo, traditionally in 1257.
In which country is Battle of Shanghai?
Battle of Shanghai: Taiwan. It resulted in the Japanese capture of Shanghai and heavy destruction to the city.

Kataeb Party: Lebanon. The Phalangists were responsible for the Black Saturday massacre, the Tel al-Zaatar massacre, Ehden massacre, and the Karantina massacre.
In which country is Chakri dynasty?
Chakri dynasty: Thailand. The Chakri dynasty, unofficially the House of Chakri, is the current reigning dynasty of the Kingdom of Thailand.
In which country was Great Smog of London?
Great Smog of London: United Kingdom. The Great Smog was a severe air pollution event that affected London, England, in December 1952.
Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Sardinia?
Kingdom of Sardinia: Italian. Beginning in 1324, James and his successors conquered the island of Sardinia and established de facto their de jure authority.
Which of these was an official language of the Aztec Empire?
Aztec Empire: Classical Nahuatl. Its people and civil society are historiographically referred to as the Aztecs or the Culhua-Mexica.
Which of these was an official language of Congo Free State?
Congo Free State: French. It was privately owned by King Leopold II, the constitutional monarch of the Kingdom of Belgium.
Which country uses the Sicilian piastra as its official currency?

The Sicilian piastra is the official currency of Kingdom of Sicily. It was a successor state of the County of Sicily, which had been founded in 1071 during the Norman conquest of the southern peninsula.
This member of the Imperial House of Japan reigned as the 125th emperor from 1989 until his abdication in 2019, with his era named the Heisei era — who is he?
Akihito (born 23 December 1933) is a member of the Imperial House of Japan who reigned as the 125th emperor of Japan from 7 January 1989 until his abdication on 30 April 2019.
This political philosophy advocates for abolishing authority and hierarchy, and is described as the libertarian wing of the socialist movement. What ideology is this?
Anarchism is a political philosophy and movement that seeks to abolish all institutions that perpetuate authority, coercion, or hierarchy, primarily targeting the state and capitalism.

Convicted as a war criminal for his role in the deportation of Dutch Jews while serving as Reichskommissar of the Netherlands, this man had briefly been Austria's chancellor before the 1938 Anschluss — who was he?

Arthur Seyss-Inquart (Austrian German; 22 July 1892 - 16 October 1946) was an Austrian Nazi politician and convicted war criminal who served as Chancellor of Austria in 1938 for two days before the Anschluss.
This 1944 amphibious assault on a Pacific island put Japan's home cities within range of B-29 bombers and triggered the resignation of Prime Minister Hideki Tōjō — which engagement?
Battle of Saipan was an amphibious assault launched by the United States against the Empire of Japan during the Pacific campaign of World War II between 15 June and 9 July 1944.
Originally a townhouse built for a duke in 1703, this London landmark was bought by George III in 1761 as a home for Queen Charlotte — what is it?
Buckingham Palace is the official residence and the administrative headquarters of the monarch of the United Kingdom in London.
Writing mainly in Russian but also in his native tongue, this author became one of the most celebrated figures in all of Kyrgyz literature — who is he?
Chinghiz Aitmatov (12 December 1928 - 10 June 2008) was a Kyrgyz author who wrote mainly in Russian, but also in Kyrgyz.
Taking office at just 35, this Ecuadorian businessman-turned-politician became the second-youngest president in his country's history. Who is he?
Daniel Noboa (born 30 November 1987) is an Ecuadorian politician and businessman serving as the 48th and current president of Ecuador since 2023.
First held on April 22, 1970, this globally coordinated annual event rallies support for environmental protection — what is it?

Earth Day is an annual event on April 22 to demonstrate support for environmental protection. This day of nature's equipoise was later sanctioned in a proclamation written by McConnell and signed by Secretary General U Thant at the United Nations.
This political position argues the EU is too bureaucratic, insufficiently democratic, and erodes national sovereignty, with its mildest form seeking reform rather than exit — what is it called?
Euroscepticism is a political position involving criticism of the European Union (EU) and European integration.
Rising from a career as a shipowner to minister for marine and colonies, this man served as President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899 — who is he?
Félix Faure (30 January 1841 - 16 February 1899) was President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899.
Triggered by the 1929 Wall Street crash, this decade-long global economic downturn brought mass unemployment to the US, UK, and Germany — name the era?
Great Depression was a severe global economic downturn from 1929 to 1939.

Raised on a farm outside Hamilton before lecturing in politics at the University of Auckland, this Labour figure went on to lead her country for nearly a decade and later ran the UN's development programme — who is she?

Helen Clark (born 26 February 1950) is a New Zealand politician who served as the 37th prime minister of New Zealand from 1999 to 2008 and was the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme from 2009 to 2017.

Leading a party called the Free Voters since 2018, this German politician serves as Bavaria's deputy minister president and its state minister for economic affairs, regional development, and energy — who is he?

Hubert Aiwanger (born 26 January 1971) is a German politician and party leader of the Free Voters since 2018, the Deputy Minister President of Bavaria and Bavarian Minister of Economic affairs, Regional Development and Energy.
A scion of a family that owns the Hyatt hotel chain, this Democratic politician has served as the 43rd governor of Illinois since 2019 — who is he?
JB Pritzker (born January 19, 1965) is an American politician, philanthropist, and businessman serving since 2019 as the 43rd governor of Illinois.

Educated at Wheaton College in the United States, this monarch became the world's youngest reigning king at age 26 when his father abdicated the throne of a small Himalayan kingdom in 2006 — who is he?
Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck (born 21 February 1980) is the current King of Bhutan, reigning since 9 December 2006.

This South African politician founded and leads a communist, black nationalist party, having previously served as president of the African National Congress's Youth League before his expulsion from the party in 2012 — who is he?
Julius Malema (born 3 March 1981) is a South African politician.

Beginning in 1881 with the crowning of a Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen prince as King Carol I and ending with King Michael I's 1947 abdication, this constitutional monarchy grew from an earlier union of Moldavia and Wallachia — which kingdom?
Kingdom of Romania was a constitutional monarchy that existed from 1881 to 1947.
Championing free speech, free assembly, market economies and the rule of law, this political philosophy centers on the rights of the individual — what is it?
Liberalism is a political and moral philosophy based on the rights of the individual, liberty, consent of the governed, political equality, right to private property, and equality before the law.
A leading Indian LGBT activist who runs the Lakshya Trust, he is the probable heir to a former Maharaja and the world's first openly gay prince — who is it?
Manvendra Singh Gohil (born 23 September 1965) is a son and probable heir of former Maharaja of Rajpipla.

Before founding Herut and Likud and becoming an Israeli prime minister, he led the militant Irgun and proclaimed a 1944 revolt against British rule, behind attacks like the King David Hotel bombing — who was he?
Menachem Begin (16 August 1913 - 9 March 1992) was an Israeli politician who founded Herut and Likud and served as prime minister of Israel from 1977 to 1983.
Serving as leader of the house in Madhya Pradesh's legislative assembly, this BJP politician became the state's Chief Minister — who is he?
Mohan Yadav (born 25 March 1965) is an Indian politician serving as the current Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh and also serving as leader of the house in legislative assembly.
Founded in Turkey in 2018 by the son of a former prime minister, this Islamist movement sees itself as heir to his father's 1990s movement and the Millî Görüş ideology — which one?
New Welfare Party is an Islamist and ultraconservative political party in Turkey, founded on 23 November 2018.
Sparked by allegations of massive fraud in a 2004 presidential runoff, this wave of protests centered on Kyiv brought political upheaval to Ukraine that winter — what event is it known as?
Orange Revolution was a series of protests that led to political upheaval in Ukraine from late November 2004 to January 2005.

This ancient people settled along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age, organizing their territory into a confederation of city-states with a language whose origins scholars still debate — who were they?
Philistines (LXX Koine) were an ancient people who lived along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age.
Worshipped as the seventh avatar of Vishnu and considered the ideal man, this Hindu deity is the hero of an ancient epic poem — who is he?
Rama is a major deity in Hinduism.
A leading theorist of Germany's SPD, she broke away to co-found the Spartacus League that became the KPD, and wrote influentially on imperialism and revolution — who is she?
Rosa Luxemburg (5 March 1871 - 15 January 1919) was a Polish and naturalised-German Marxist theorist and revolutionary.
In Egyptian mythology, this warrior goddess also presided over medicine, carried the epithet 'the eye of Ra' as a solar deity, and was closely linked with the goddesses Hathor and Bastet. Who is she?
Sekhmet (or Sachmis, from Ancient) is a warrior goddess as well as goddess of medicine.
Serving as the 39th US vice president before resigning in 1973 under Richard Nixon, this politician was only the second VP in history to resign — the first was John C. Calhoun in 1832 — who was he?
Spiro Agnew (November 9, 1918 - September 17, 1996) was the 39th vice president of the United States, serving from 1969 until his resignation in 1973 under President Richard Nixon.
This divine hero of Greek mythology, raised by his mother Aethra and said to be the son of either the king of Athens or the sea god Poseidon, is famed for slaying the Minotaur — who is he?
Theseus (Ancient) was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur.
This Roman goddess of love and beauty was said to be the ancestor of the Roman people through her son Aeneas, who fled the fall of Troy. Who is she?
Venus (mythology) (Classical) is a Roman goddess whose functions encompass love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity, and victory.
A fierce opponent of slavery's spread, this Secretary of State served the Union through the Civil War and negotiated the treaty to buy Alaska. Who was he?

William H. Seward (May 16, 1801 - October 10, 1872) was an American politician who served as United States Secretary of State from 1861 to 1869 and earlier served as governor of New York and as a United States senator.
Elected in 2007 to the nine-member Politburo Standing Committee, the Chinese Communist Party's top decision-making body, this former senior leader once wielded major power in Beijing — who is he?
Zhou Yongkang (born December 3, 1942) is a former senior leader of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Allegedly the first Syrian to hold the position, this militant leader served as the fourth so-called caliph of the Islamic State from November 2022 until his death in April 2023. Who was he?
Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi: Islamic State leader from 2022 to 2023.
A nephew and son-in-law of his predecessor Jalaluddin, this Delhi Sultan fended off several Mongol invasions and overhauled revenue and price-control policy from 1296 to 1316 — who was he?

Alauddin Khalji: Sultan of Delhi from 1296 to 1316. Alauddin Khalji (Persian: علاء الدین خلجی; born Ali Gurshasp; c. 1266 – 4 January 1316) was the Khalji dynasty Sultan of Delhi from 1296 until his death in 1316.
Known to local tribespeople as the 'hero of the jungle,' this Indian revolutionary led a 1922 guerrilla rebellion against British rule in the Andhra-Odisha borderlands — who is he?
Alluri Sitarama Raju: Indian freedom fighter and revolutionary.
Serving as Governor of Jakarta before running for president in 2024, this Indonesian politician founded a program that sends university graduates to teach for a year nationwide — who is he?

Falling on the tenth day of the first month of the Islamic calendar, this commemoration is marked by Sunni Muslims with voluntary fasting, recalling events like Moses parting the Red Sea and Noah leaving the Ark — what is it?
Ashura: Tenth day of the Islamic month of Muharram. Ashura is celebrated in Sunni Islam through supererogatory fasting and other acceptable expressions of joy.

Fluent in Cherokee, Choctaw, and several other Native languages, this man escaped slavery and went on to rack up over 3,000 arrests as one of the first Black deputy U.S. Marshals west of the Mississippi — who was he?

Drawing on Bolshevism and anarchism, this Indian revolutionary's largely symbolic bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly and a jail hunger strike made him a folk hero — and a martyr after his execution at age 23; who was he?
Practiced by early humans and often paired with a funeral ceremony, this method of laying the dead to rest involves placing a body into the ground or a mausoleum — what is it?
Burial: Ritual act of placing a dead person or animal into the ground.

In 1989, the assault of a young woman running through a Manhattan green space led to the conviction — and eventual exoneration — of five teenagers now known as the Exonerated Five. What is this notorious incident known as?
Central Park jogger case: 1989 crime in New York City.

A West Virginia farm boy who started WWII as an Army private and aircraft mechanic before becoming a flying ace, in October 1947 he became the first pilot confirmed to break the sound barrier in level flight — who was he?
Chuck Yeager: American flying ace and test pilot (1923–2020)

Marching his 13th Legion over a forbidden river into Italy in January 49 BC, Julius Caesar defied the Senate and triggered a civil war that made him dictator for life — this act gave its name to what idiom for a point of no return?
Crossing the Rubicon: Idiom meaning a point of no return. Caesar was not allowed to command an army within Italy proper, and by crossing the river with his forces was defying law and risking death.
Bribed by Philistine lords to learn the secret of a mighty Nazirite's strength, this biblical woman finally coaxed out the truth about his hair — who is she?
Delilah: Woman in the Book of Judges of the Hebrew Bible.
First ruled from 918 by Richard the Justiciar and later inherited by a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty, which feudal territory belonged to the medieval Kingdom of France?
Duchy of Burgundy: Vassal territory of France, 918–1482.
Centered in what is now southwestern Iran, with its capital at Susa, this Bronze Age civilization was known to classical writers as Susiana. What was this ancient Near Eastern civilization called?
Elam: Ancient pre-Iranian civilization between 3200 and 539 BC.
A five-time Socialist Party candidate for U.S. president, this labor leader co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and led a major railway strike against the CB&Q line in 1888. Who is he?
Eugene V. Debs: American labor and political leader (1855–1926)
It erupted in 1989 when Charles Taylor's NPFL invaded from Ivory Coast to topple President Samuel Doe, who was soon captured and executed by a splinter faction — which conflict is this?
First Liberian Civil War: 1989–1997 war in West Africa.
According to Galatians chapter 5, nine virtues — including love, joy, peace, and self-control — mark a life lived in step with God's presence; what biblical term describes this list?
Fruit of the Holy Spirit: Biblical term.
Meaning 'the one who yawns' in Mescalero-Chiricahua, this name belonged to the Bedonkohe Apache medicine man who led raids against Mexican and U.S. forces from 1850 to 1886. Who was he?
Geronimo: Leader of the Bedonkohe Apache (1829–1909)
One of the original Mercury Seven, this astronaut became the second American in space in 1961 and later commanded Gemini and Apollo missions — who is he?
Ruling from the mountain fortress of Alamut from 1090, this founder of the Order of Assassins was dubbed the 'Old Man of the Mountain' by Marco Polo — who was he?
Hasan-i Sabbah: Ismaili religious and military leader (c. 1050–1124)
This reclusive Afghan cleric has almost no digital footprint beyond two photographs and a few audio recordings, yet has led his country's ruling movement since 2016 — who is he?
Hibatullah Akhundzada: Supreme Leader of Afghanistan since 2021.
This grandson of Genghis, whose army sacked Baghdad in the 13th century and ended the Abbasid dynasty, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia — who was he?
Hulegu Khan: Western Asian Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265)
The first Muslim president of Guyana, this politician was sworn in during August 2020 after a lengthy recount dispute and later won a second term — who is he?
Irfaan Ali: President of Guyana since 2020. Mohamed Irfaan Ali (born 25 April 1980) is a Guyanese politician serving as the tenth and current president of Guyana since 2020.

Raised in the wealthy capital of Gurganj, this able general became the last Khwarazmshah of the Anushtegin dynasty, succeeding his father even as a younger brother — backed by the powerful Queen Mother — contested his claim. Who is he?
Jalal al-Din Mangburni: Last shah of the Khwarazmian Empire from 1220 to 1231.
A protégé of Martin Luther King Jr., this Baptist minister and civil rights leader founded the organizations that merged into the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition — who is he?
Jesse Jackson: American minister, activist and politician (1941–2026)
This English actor played the third incarnation of the Doctor on a beloved sci-fi series in the 1970s and later starred as a scarecrow brought to life in another family show — who is he?
This Polish statesman served as Chief of State after World War I and is regarded as the father of the Second Republic, re-established in 1918 after 123 years of partition. Who was he?

Named after a 1954 Ilya Ehrenburg novel, this mid-1950s-to-mid-1960s period saw Soviet censorship and repression relax following Stalin's death and the 'Secret Speech' denouncing him — what's it called?
Khrushchev thaw: Period of Soviet history, 1950s-60s.
Founded by Anton LaVey with the 1966 creation of the Church of Satan in San Francisco, this belief system blends humanism, hedonism, and showmanship, drawing on Nietzsche and Ayn Rand — what is it?
LaVeyan Satanism: Religious movement founded by Anton LaVey.
Revered as Quaid-e-Millat, "Leader of the Nation," this lawyer-statesman became his country's first prime minister in 1947 and was assassinated four years later. Who was he?
Liaquat Ali Khan: Prime Minister of Pakistan from 1947 to 1951.
This three-time French Prime Minister led the left-wing Popular Front government in the 1930s and later became a staunch opponent of the Vichy regime — who was he?
The first Filipino to lead a government over the entire Philippines, this president defeated Emilio Aguinaldo in the 1935 election and lent his name to a city in Metro Manila — who was he?
Manuel L. Quezon: President of the Philippines from 1935 to 1944.
The daughter of a former Pakistani prime minister, this politician made history in February 2024 as the first woman to become chief minister of Punjab — who is she?
Maryam Nawaz: Chief Minister of Punjab (born 1973)
He recovered Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261 and founded the dynasty that would rule the Byzantines until the city finally fell in 1453 — which emperor?
Michael VIII Palaiologos: Byzantine emperor from 1261 to 1282.
This Iranian prime minister's land reforms and social security programs ended abruptly in a 1953 coup engineered by the CIA and MI6 — who was he?
Mohammad Mosaddegh: Prime Minister of Iran from 1951 to 1953.
Serving as Israel's prime minister from 2021 to 2022, this politician and former special-forces soldier co-founded the tech company Cyota after growing up in Haifa — who is he?
Naftali Bennett: Prime Minister of Israel from 2021 to 2022. Bennett has served as the head of Bennett 2026 since 2025; the party is allied with Yesh Atid as part of an alliance called Together.
From 1965 to 1977 this Ukrainian-born official served as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet — effectively the Soviet head of state. Who was he?

Announced by President Bush after the September 11 attacks, this was the official U.S. name for the first phase (2001-2014) of the Afghanistan war against al-Qaeda and the Taliban — what was it called?
Operation Enduring Freedom: Official name for the US's war on terror.
Known for championing charter schools, this former superintendent led school districts in Philadelphia and Chicago before running — and narrowly losing — a bid for Chicago mayor in 2023. Who is he?
Paul Vallas: American politician and school administrator (born 1953)
A protégé of the dictator Sulla, this Roman general and statesman celebrated three triumphs and was elected consul on three separate occasions during the late Republic — who was he?
Pompey: Roman general and statesman (106–48 BC)
In October 2021, this U.S. assistant secretary for health became the nation's first openly transgender four-star officer across all eight uniformed services — who is she?
Rachel Levine: American public health official (born 1957)

This short-lived 1990s state in the Balkans seceded from a disintegrating Yugoslavia in 1992, triggering a three-year war as rival Serb and Croat factions carved out their own unrecognized quasi-states — what state?
Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Balkan country (1992–1995)
Born in Tampico, Illinois, this future actor started as a sports broadcaster in Iowa in 1933 before moving to Hollywood and later serving as Screen Actors Guild president twice. Who was he?
Ronald Reagan: President of the United States from 1981 to 1989.
Nominated by President George W. Bush in 2005, this jurist became just the second Italian American justice on the Supreme Court, after Antonin Scalia — who is he?
Samuel Alito: US Supreme Court justice since 2006.

Once Adolf Hitler's personal chauffeur and bodyguard, this German officer rose to become the highest-ranking commissioned commander in the Waffen-SS despite having no formal staff training — who is he?
Sepp Dietrich: German Nazi politician and SS commander (1892–1966)

Lasting 872 days and killing an estimated 1.5 million from a prewar population of 3.2 million, this WWII blockade of the Soviet Union's second-largest city was never successfully captured — what was it?
Siege of Leningrad: Blockade by the Axis powers, 1941–1944.

Daughter of Darius III of Persia, she was captured after her father's defeat at Issus and became the second bride of the Macedonian conqueror at the Susa weddings in 324 BC, before being killed by his other spouse, Roxana — who was she?
Stateira (wife of Alexander the Great): Daughter of Darius III, died 323 BC.
A Thai Chinese general, he became the only king of Thonburi after leading the liberation of Siam from Burmese occupation and reuniting a country splintered among warlords — who was he?
Taksin: King of Siam from 1767 to 1782.

A protégé of Robert Walpole, this Whig statesman served as a Secretary of State for 30 unbroken years and dominated British foreign policy — and was twice Prime Minister. By which dukedom is he commonly known?
Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle: Prime Minister of Great Britain (1754–1756; 1757–1762)
This Indian politician served as Maharashtra's 19th chief minister from 2019 to 2022 while also editing a newspaper for over a decade — who is he?
Uddhav Thackeray: 19th Chief Minister of Maharashtra from 2019 to 2022 (born 1960)
In 1976, this Soviet pilot defected to the West by flying his MiG-25 'Foxbat' jet interceptor to Japan, handing the CIA what George H. W. Bush called an 'intelligence bonanza' — who is he?
Viktor Belenko: Soviet pilot who defected to the West (1947–2023)
One of the most popular presidents at his death in 1923, this Ohio newspaperman who built up the Marion Star saw his reputation later wrecked by exposed scandals — who was he?
Warren G. Harding: President of the United States from 1921 to 1923.
Raging from 1914 to 1918 and nicknamed 'the Great War,' this conflict's mass troop movements helped spread the deadly Spanish flu pandemic — which war?
World War I: 1914–1918 global conflict. The war saw important developments in weaponry including tanks, aircraft, artillery, machine guns, and chemical weapons.
This late-Qing statesman raised and organized the Xiang Army to crush the Taiping Rebellion and helped launch the Tongzhi Restoration — who was he?
Zeng Guofan: Chinese politician and military commander (1811–1872)

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.

Which of these is a chemist?
Ellen Swallow Richards is a chemist. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
What is the atomic number of Moscovium?
Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.
What is the atomic number of Bismuth?
Bismuth is a chemical element; it has symbol Bi and atomic number 83.
In what year did Marie Curie die?
Marie Curie: Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
In what year was Sodium discovered?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
Ammonium chloride: Pfizer. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.
Boeing 777X: United States. The Boeing 777X is an American long-range, wide-body, twin-engine airliner built by Boeing Commercial Airplanes, undergoing flight testing.
Who is credited with discovering Telescopium?
Telescopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is a Latinized form of the Greek word for telescope.
Who is credited with discovering Spontaneous generation?
Spontaneous generation: Anaximander. It was hypothesized that certain forms, such as fleas, could arise from inanimate matter such as dust, or that maggots could arise from dead flesh.
Who is credited with discovering SN 1987A?
SN 1987A: Ian Shelton. SN 1987A was a Type II supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
This Onmyōdō master advised Heian emperors on astrology and spiritual matters; a Kyoto shrine and an Osaka train station now honor him — who is he?
Abe no Seimei (February 21, 921 AD - October 31, 1005) was a Japanese onmyji, a court official and specialist of Onmyd, during the middle of the Heian period.
First approved in the United States in 1966, this xanthine oxidase inhibitor treats high uric acid levels linked to gout, kidney stones, and chemotherapy — what medication is it?
Allopurinol is a medication used to decrease high blood uric acid levels.
Nicknamed 'the heart of the scorpion,' this distinctly reddish variable star is the brightest in the constellation Scorpius — what is it?
Antares is the brightest star in the constellation of Scorpius. It has the Bayer designation α Scorpii, which is Latinised to Alpha Scorpii.

Named for the Ancient Greek word for 'star' after its flower shape, this group of roughly 170 mostly Eurasian perennial plants is also known for its late-blooming 'Michaelmas daisies' — which plant group?
Aster (genus) is a genus of perennial flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.
Once chairman of the Nasdaq, this financier admitted to masterminding the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, estimated at $65 billion — who was he?

Bernie Madoff (April 29, 1938 - April 14, 2021) was an American financier, con artist, and stock broker who was the admitted mastermind of the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, worth an estimated $65 billion.
This family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, sheep, and goats across 143 living species — name the family?
Bovidae is the biological family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals that includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, and goat-antelopes such as sheep and goats.
Sole living family in the mammalian suborder Tylopoda, which group unites camels with llamas and their South American relatives?
Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
A secondarily aquatic clade within the order that also includes hippos, this infraorder covers whales, dolphins and porpoises, along with extinct relatives like Basilosaurus — which group of animals?

Cetacean are marine mammals belonging to the infraorder Cetacea, a secondarily aquatic clade under the order Artiodactyla that include whales, dolphins, porpoises and extinct groups such as Basilosaurus.

From a tree in the myrtle family, these dried flower buds from the Moluccas are harvested year-round across different countries and lend their scent to everything from cosmetics to cooking — what are they?
Clove are the aromatic flower buds of a tree in the family Myrtaceae, Syzygium aromaticum.

This naturally occurring but largely inactive steroid hormone shields organs like the kidneys from active cortisol, and gets converted back into cortisol by an enzyme mainly in the liver — what hormone is it?
Cortisone is a naturally occurring, mostly inactive pregnene (21-carbon) steroid hormone.
The word names both a noun — a plan or proposal made by a thinking agent — and a verb for developing one, always aiming to satisfy goals while weighing function and aesthetics; what is it?
Design is the concept or proposal for an object, process, or system.
This soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida is also known by slang names like 'dew-worm,' 'rainworm,' and 'nightcrawler.' What creature is it?
Earthworm is a soil-dwelling terrestrial invertebrate that belongs to the phylum Annelida.

A German Jew who fled the Nazi regime for the United States, this social psychologist and psychoanalyst co-founded a New York psychiatric institute and was associated with the Frankfurt School of critical theory — who is he?
Erich Fromm (March 23, 1900 - March 18, 1980) was a German-American social psychologist, psychoanalyst, sociologist, humanistic philosopher, and democratic socialist.
Bred in Brazil as a guard dog, cattle herder, and big-game hunter, this large mastiff-type breed was also once used to catch runaway slaves — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.

Cataloged by the astronomer Ptolemy in the second century AD and still one of the 88 modern constellations, this zodiac constellation takes its Latin name from the mythological twins Castor and Pollux — what's the constellation?
Gemini (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac and is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.

Native to the Amazon basin, this climbing plant's coffee-bean-sized seeds can contain up to 6% caffeine — roughly double the concentration found in green coffee beans — and flavor a popular Brazilian soft drink. Name the plant?
Guarana (from the Portuguese guaran; Paullinia cupana, syns.

This colorless, nearly odorless organic compound is a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms, widely used as a cheap, largely unreactive solvent and found in small amounts in modern gasoline blends — what is it?
Hexane is an organic compound, a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms and the molecular formula C6H14.
This medical condition occurs when the body, or a region of it, is deprived of adequate oxygen at the tissue level — what is it called?

Hypoxia (medicine) is a condition in which the body or a region of the body is deprived of an adequate oxygen supply at the tissue level. Hypoxia may be classified as either generalized, affecting the whole body, or local, affecting a region of the body.

This English mathematician made foundational contributions to matrix and invariant theory, founded the American Journal of Mathematics at Johns Hopkins, and was teaching at Oxford when he died. Who was he?
James Joseph Sylvester (3 September 1814 - 15 March 1897) was an English mathematician.

The first woman of Indian origin to fly to space, this astronaut and aerospace engineer first studied in India before earning advanced degrees in the US and flying aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1997 — who was she?
Kalpana Chawla (July 1, 1962 - February 1, 2003) was an Indian-American astronaut and aerospace engineer who was the first woman of Indian origin to fly to space.
This small Arctic rodent is a key prey source for tundra carnivores and is the subject of a persistent myth that it marches off cliffs in mass suicide — what animal is it?
Lemming is a small rodent, usually found in or near the Arctic in tundra biomes.
Named for a Dutch physicist, this six-parameter family of linear equations converts spacetime coordinates between reference frames moving at constant relative velocity — what is it?
Lorentz transformation are a six-parameter family of linear transformations from a coordinate frame in spacetime to another frame that moves at a constant velocity relative to the former.

A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered a new element in 1939 by purifying lanthanum laced with actinium, and went on to become the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?
Marguerite Perey (19 October 1909 - 13 May 1975) was a French physicist and a student of Marie Curie.

This American theoretical physicist and science communicator, a professor at the City College of New York, won a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for a famous science-fiction author, honoring his work bridging science and sci-fi. Who is he?
Michio Kaku (born January 24, 1947) is an American theoretical physicist, science communicator, futurologist, and writer of popular science.
Scholars can't even agree on which elements define it, yet it appears in every human society as a vehicle for creativity through composition and performance — what is it?
Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, or otherwise expressive content.
A highly corrosive mineral compound with the formula HNO3, this strong inorganic acid is colorless but yellows over time as it decomposes. What is this acid?
Nitric acid is an inorganic compound with the formula HNO3. The compound is colorless, but samples tend to acquire a yellow cast over time due to decomposition into oxides of nitrogen.
This systemic skeletal disorder develops when the rate of bone breakdown outpaces new bone formation with age, leaving bones porous, less dense, and prone to fracture — what's the condition called?
Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by low bone mass, micro-architectural deterioration of bone tissue leading to more porous bone, and consequent increase in fracture risk.
Brought on by too little niacin, this disease announces itself with the 'three D's' — dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and dementia — what is it?
Pellagra is a disease caused by a lack of the vitamin niacin (vitamin B3).
Which condition, more common in people with obesity or a family history, involves hair and skin debris being drawn into tissue through tiny skin openings called pits?
Pilonidal disease is a type of skin infection that typically occurs as a cyst between the cheeks of the buttocks and often at the upper end.

This corticosteroid drug treats a huge range of conditions — from rheumatoid arthritis and asthma to eye inflammation and certain cancers — and can be taken orally, injected, or applied to the skin. What is it?
Prednisolone is a corticosteroid, a steroid hormone used to treat certain types of allergies, inflammatory conditions, autoimmune disorders, and cancers, electrolyte imbalances, and skin conditions.
This root vegetable in the mustard family, whose entire plant (leaves included) is edible, was domesticated in Asia and is now grown worldwide — what vegetable is it?
Radish (Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp.
This big, sociable black corvid is told apart from its relatives by a bare, whitish patch on its face, and it nests in noisy treetop colonies near farms and villages — which bird is it?
Rook (bird) (Corvus frugilegus) is a member of the family Corvidae in the passerine order of birds.

These pinnipeds, distinguished from true seals by their external ear flaps and ability to walk on all fours, belong to the eared-seal family alongside fur seals, with six living species worldwide. What animal is this?
Sea lion are pinnipeds characterized by external ear flaps, long foreflippers, the ability to walk on all fours, short and thick hair, and a big chest and belly.

Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'soap,' this cheesy secretion of shed skin cells, oils, and moisture collects under the foreskin in males and around the folds of female genitalia — what is it called?
Smegma (from Ancient Greek, smgma, 'soap') is a cheesy substance composed of shed skin cells, skin oils, and moisture that occurs in male and female mammalian genitalia.
A Canadian cognitive psychologist at Harvard who champions evolutionary psychology and the computational theory of mind, which popular-science author wrote on how children learn irregular verb forms?
Steven Pinker (born September 18, 1954) is a Canadian cognitive psychologist, psycholinguist, popular science author, and public intellectual.
This protective cap of repetitive nucleotide sequences guards the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes from progressive degradation — what is it called?
Telomere (from Ancient Greek (tlos) 'end' and (mros) 'part') is a region of repetitive nucleotide sequences associated with specialized proteins at the ends of linear chromosomes (see Sequences).
Divided into the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, this core section of the body is where the head, neck, and all four limbs attach — which body part?
Torso is the central part, or the core, of the body of many animals (including human beings), from which the head, neck, limbs, tail and other appendages extend.
Measuring under five feet long, this critically endangered porpoise is endemic to a small corner of Mexico's Baja California coast — which species?
Vaquita (v-; Phocoena sinus) is a species of porpoise endemic to the northern end of the Gulf of California in Baja California, Mexico.
Inspired by the code-breaking game Mastermind, this once-a-day puzzle gives you six tries and colored tiles to crack the same word everyone else is solving — which game?
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
Wordle is a web-based word game created and developed by the Welsh software engineer Josh Wardle.
This mucolytic drug is the go-to antidote for acetaminophen overdose, working by boosting glutathione to neutralize the drug's toxic byproducts — what is it?
Acetylcysteine: Medication used to treat overdose of paracetamol.
Twice President of the Swiss Confederation, this Social Democratic politician left the Federal Council in 2023 to become Secretary General of the Council of Europe — who is he?
Alain Berset: Swiss Federal Councillor from 2012 to 2023.
Nicknamed the boto for its rosy pink hue (especially in males), this South American toothed whale is the largest species of its kind found in a freshwater habitat — what is it?
Amazon river dolphin: Species of toothed whale. The position of the Araguaian river dolphin (I. araguaiaensis) within the clade is still unclear.
Comprising over 22,000 species including ragworms, earthworms, and leeches, this phylum of segmented worms use parapodia to move — what is it?
Annelid: Phylum of segmented worms. The basic annelid form consists of multiple segments called metameres.

Known only from fragmentary remains including vertebrae and a giant femur first found by a farmer in 1987, this titanosaur may be the largest land animal ever discovered, stretching up to 35 meters — which genus?
Argentinosaurus: Late Cretaceous giant sauropod dinosaur genus.
This broad category of technology uses machines and predetermined rules to reduce the need for human intervention in factories, boilers, and telephone switching — what is it?
Automation: Use of various control systems for operating equipment.

Nicknamed 'Huey,' this American utility helicopter became the first turbine-powered rotorcraft in U.S. military service, developed in the 1950s to meet an Army need for medical evacuation and utility missions. Which aircraft?
Bell UH-1 Iroquois: Huey family of American military utility helicopters.
This medical term for blood escaping the circulatory system describes a healthy person as able to lose 10 to 15 percent of their total volume without serious harm — what is it called?
Bleeding: Blood escaping from the circulatory system. Bleeding, hemorrhage, haemorrhage or blood loss, is blood escaping from the circulatory system from damaged blood vessels.
Typically about two-thirds copper and one-third zinc, which prehistoric substitutional alloy differs from bronze, which swaps in tin instead of zinc?
Brass: Alloy of copper and zinc. Brass has long been popular for its bright, golden appearance and is used for drawer pulls and doorknobs.
The world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance works by mimicking adenosine's shape and blocking its receptors, keeping you awake — what is this stimulant?

This German-Swedish pharmacist had a knack for discovery — molybdenum, tungsten, barium, chlorine, and arguably oxygen all trace to his bench — but the same hands-on chemistry may have killed him via mercury poisoning. Which unlucky genius is it?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele: Swedish German chemist who discovered oxygen (1742–1786)
Descended from land mammals but now fully aquatic, this group swims via up-and-down tail strokes and includes toothed members capable of echolocation — what group includes whales and dolphins?
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Named for an Indonesian island where an 18th-century naturalist first catalogued it, this pungent, oregano-scented succulent also goes by Cuban oregano and Indian borage — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus: Species of plant. Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Latin for 'raven,' this widely distributed bird genus includes crows and rooks and gave a group of its members the eerie collective noun 'a murder' — what genus is it?
Corvus: Genus of birds including crows, ravens and rooks.

First synthesized in 1874, this insecticide earned its discoverer a 1948 Nobel Prize and was used in WWII against malaria and typhus before becoming infamous for its environmental damage — what is it?
DDT: Organochloride known as an insecticide.
Sold under the brand name Valium, this benzodiazepine anxiolytic treats anxiety, seizures, alcohol withdrawal, and muscle spasms — and can even induce memory loss during procedures; what is it?
Diazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
Marketed as Cymbalta, this serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor treats depression, anxiety, and fibromyalgia pain — what is it?
Born in Pretoria and once a Zip2 co-founder, this CEO of Tesla and SpaceX became, by some estimates, the first dollar trillionaire in 2026 — who is he?
Elon Musk: Businessman and public official (born 1971)
Also called moral philosophy, this field splits into normative, applied, and meta- branches as it asks what people ought to do and whether objective moral facts even exist. Which discipline is it?
Birds of prey in the genus Falco, some small species are called hobbies and hover-hunters are called kestrels — what are they collectively known as?
Falcon: Birds of prey in the genus Falco. The largest falcon is the gyrfalcon at up to 65 cm (26 in) in length.
Discovered in Dubna in 1999, this superheavy synthetic element (number 114) honors a Russian physicist whose name in Cyrillic explains why its spelling swaps a 'yo' for an 'e' — which element?
Flerovium: Chemical element with atomic number 114 (Fl)
Named in 1753 from Greek words for 'milk' and 'flower,' this genus of about 20 bulbous perennial species is better known by its common name, snowdrop — what is its scientific genus?
Galanthus: Genus of flowering plants in the family Amaryllidacee.

Likely first domesticated by Austronesian peoples in Maritime Southeast Asia, this herbaceous perennial is grown for the spicy rhizome that puts it in the same family as turmeric and cardamom — what is it?
Ginger: Species of plant used as a spice.
This junctional area between the torso and thigh, where the lower abdominal wall meets the leg, is commonly strained in a familiar sports injury — what is it called?
Groin: Area between the torso and the thigh. In human anatomy, the groin, also known as the inguinal region or iliac region, is the junctional area between the torso and the thigh.

Often defined as the normal functioning of the body free of disease, pain, or injury, this multidimensional state of well-being can be promoted by exercise and sleep and harmed by smoking or stress — what's the one-word concept?
Health: Desirable level of functional or metabolic efficiency of a living being.
Named for the English physician who first described it in 1832, this cancer is defined by multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes — what is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of blood and immune-system cancer.
This immune response causes tissue damage upon repeated exposure to an antigen and underlies conditions like hay fever, which affects roughly one in ten people worldwide — what is it called?
Hypersensitivity: Overreaction of the immune system to an antigen.
More than half of all animal species belong to this one chitinous-shelled group, each member sporting three body parts and three pairs of jointed legs — who are they?
Caused by a buildup of bilirubin, this condition turns the skin and eyes yellowish and affects an estimated 80% of newborns in their first week of life — what is it?
Jaundice: Abnormal yellowish skin colour caused by high level of bilirubin.
This genus of coniferous trees and shrubs in the cypress family includes a species that forms the world's highest-known forest, at 4,900 metres in the Himalayas — what is it called?
Derived from the design of the Vought F-8 Crusader, this subsonic carrier-based light attack aircraft replaced the Douglas Skyhawk and saw extensive action in the Vietnam War — which aircraft?
LTV A-7 Corsair II: American attack aircraft family.
This Chinese herbalist, martial artist, and tactical advisor died in 1933 having allegedly been born in 1677 — a longevity claim gerontologists dismiss as myth. Who was he?
Li Ching-Yuen: Chinese herbalist (died 1933). Li's year of birth was alleged to be 1677, though his true age has never been determined.

Credited as a 'Father of Cinematography,' this French artist filmed the Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds in 1888 — then vanished without a trace two years later, and his work never shaped commercial cinema. Who was he?
Louis Le Prince: French motion-picture pioneer (1841–1890s)
Distinguished from living elephants by spirally twisted tusks and a thick coat of fur for cold climates, this extinct genus survived from the late Miocene until roughly 4,000 years ago — what was it?
Mammoth: Extinct genus of mammals. The oldest mammoth representative, Mammuthus subplanifrons, appeared around 6 million years ago during the late Miocene in southern and Eastern Africa.
Diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, treatment and palliation of injury and disease — drawing on biomedical science, genetics and technology — define this science and practice. What is it?

Medicine: Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of illness. Medicine encompasses a variety of health care practices which evolved to maintain and restore health through the prevention and treatment of illness and infection.
This scientific field studies microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and protists, encompassing sub-disciplines like virology and mycology — which discipline?
Known as simple sugars, these colorless, water-soluble crystalline compounds include glucose and fructose and serve as the building blocks of starch and cellulose — what are they called?
Monosaccharide: Simple sugars such as glucose and fructose.

This inner-ear condition brings on episodes of vertigo, ringing in the ears, and hearing loss lasting anywhere from 20 minutes to several hours — believed to stem from fluid buildup in the labyrinth. What is it?
Ménière's disease: Disorder of the inner ear. The hearing loss and ringing in the ears can become constant over time.
Its name literally means 'blue cow,' though only the males actually sport a bluish-grey coat — which is the largest antelope species in Asia?
A Boston physician, medical reformer, and 'fireside' poet, this polymath delighted readers with his 'Breakfast-Table' series begun in 1858. Who was he?
Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.: American poet, essayist, physician (1809–1894)
With long dense grey fur and rounded ears set oddly low on the sides of its head, this small wild cat — first described in 1776 near Lake Baikal — roams the cold steppes of Central Asia. What is it?
Pallas's cat: Species of small wild cat. Pallas's cat (Otocolobus manul), also called manul, is a small wild cat with long and dense light grey fur, and rounded ears set low on the sides of the head.
This bony ring connects the spine to the lower limbs at the hip joints, formed by the sacrum, coccyx, and a pair of hip bones — what body region?
Pelvis: Lower torso of the human body.
Whether captured chemically on light-sensitive film or electronically by an image sensor, this art is fundamentally the practice of recording light — what is it?
Photography: Art and practice of creating images by recording light.
Whether natural silk or synthetic nylon, this class of polymer is defined by repeating units joined through amide bonds — what is it?
Polyamide: Macromolecule with repeating units linked by amide bonds.

Native to western Eurasia and a member of the rose family, this species — the wild or sweet cherry — is the ancestor of the sour cherry, though every part of the plant except its ripe fruit is mildly toxic. What is it called?
Prunus avium: Species of flowering plant in the rose family. The species is often cultivated as an ornamental tree.
Also known as hexogen, this nitroamine explosive is the key energetic agent in C-4 and a core ingredient of Semtex — which compound?
RDX: Explosive chemical compound. RDX (Research Department Explosive or Royal Demolition Explosive), or hexogen, also known by other names, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2N2O2)3.
This branch of medicine handles more than 100 inflammatory diseases of the bones, muscles, and joints — like lupus and arthritis — and overlaps heavily with immunology. What is it?
Rheumatology: Medical speciality of inflammatory diseases.
Co-founder and first president of Mattel, she dreamed up a certain doll in 1959 and was later portrayed in the 2023 Barbie film — who was she?
Ruth Handler: American business magnate and inventor (1916–2002)
Exceeding 30 centimeters in length, this centipede from South America is the largest of its kind, preying on animals as large as small mammals and reptiles — which species?

Scolopendra gigantea: Species of Chilopoda (centipede). Scolopendra gigantea, also known as the Peruvian giant yellow-leg centipede or Amazonian giant centipede, is a centipede in the genus Scolopendra.
Made up of the collarbone, the scapula, and the upper-arm bone meeting in a ball-and-socket joint, which body part lets the arm swing in a full circle?
Shoulder: Part of the body. The articulations between the bones of the shoulder make up the shoulder joints.
Mostly made from potato starch but also found in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only at one hydroxyl group. What is it?

In probability theory, this mathematical concept models a family of random variables indexed often by time, used to describe things like bacterial growth or a gas molecule's erratic path — what is it called?
Stochastic process: Collection of random variables. Stochastic processes are widely used as mathematical models of systems and phenomena that appear to vary in a random manner.
This medical term describes a resting heart rate that exceeds 100 beats per minute — what is it?
Tachycardia: Heart rate exceeding normal resting rate.
The principal bitter alkaloid of the cacao plant, this caffeine cousin is found in chocolate, tea, and the kola nut, and works by blocking adenosine receptors. What is it?
Theobromine: Bitter alkaloid of the cacao plant. Theobromine, also known as xantheose, is the principal alkaloid of Theobroma cacao (cacao plant).
Caused by bacteria producing acid that breaks down enamel, dentin, and cementum, this common condition can turn dental cavities anywhere from yellow to black — what is it?
Tooth decay: Deformation of teeth due to acids produced by bacteria.

This orally contracted disease, caused by Salmonella Typhi bacteria, typically begins six to 30 days after exposure with a gradual high fever, weakness, and abdominal pain. Severe cases may produce distinctive rose-colored skin spots. What is this illness?

Typhoid fever: Disease caused by the bacteria Salmonella Typhi. Typhoid fever, also known as typhoid, is an orally contracted disease caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteria, also called Salmonella Typhi.
Every snake in this venomous family wields unusually long, hinged fangs for deep envenomation — and many give live birth, a trait echoed in their Latin-rooted name. What snakes are these?
Viper: Family of snakes. The earliest known vipers are believed to have diverged from the rest of the clade Caenophidia in the early Eocene.
In 1879 at the University of Leipzig, this German scholar founded the first formal psychology laboratory, earning him the title 'father of experimental psychology' — who is he?
Wilhelm Wundt: German founder of psychology (1832–1920)
Known on the street as flakka or gravel, this synthetic stimulant of the cathinone class was developed in the 1960s and later sold as a designer drug — what is it?
The symbol for iridium is Ir. Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.

Al Pacino: Alfredo James Pacino ( pə-CHEE-noh; Italian: [paˈtʃiːno]; born April 25, 1940) is an American actor.

Ethan Hawke: Ethan Green Hawke (born November 6, 1970) is an American actor, author, and filmmaker whose career on both stage and screen has spanned four decades.

Carrie Fisher: Carrie Frances Fisher (October 21, 1956 – December 27, 2016) was an American actress and writer.

WALL-E: The film follows a solitary robot named WALL-E on a future, uninhabitable, deserted Earth in 2805, left to clean up garbage.
